Mihir Sharma

I’m Mihir Sharma, an independent HCI researcher with a background in product and interaction design. My research interests lie in haptic and wearable interfaces and human–AI interaction, particularly for blind and low-vision people. Today’s assistive AI tools communicate almost entirely through speech, yet many blind and low-vision people also rely on hearing to stay aware of their surroundings. I study what information touch can convey, when a device should interrupt, and how it can communicate uncertainty.

Currently, I am working on:

  • encoding AI answers as vibration patterns that blind and low-vision people can learn (Can a Buzz Answer That?, under review at ACM IUI 2027)
  • limiting how often a wearable buzzes its wearer by mistake (TrueTap, under review at PACM IMWUT)
  • measuring whether people act on AI confidence they feel rather than see (Material Confidence, under review at ACM CHIIR 2027)
  • deciding what a navigation assistant should tell blind and low-vision pedestrians, and when (SenseShift, in progress)

I received my MFA in User Experience Design, with Distinction, from the College for Creative Studies, Detroit, advised by Prof. Predrag K. Nikolić. My thesis, TactileGrip, embedded real-time sensing and feedback in climbing holds. An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor sampled every 50 ms drives a proximity beep that quickens from 50 cm to 5 cm; contact cuts the beep and fires a single vibration pulse; pulse-gated star holds announce progress aloud, all on an Arduino Nano inside the hold. I designed it from 20 interviews with blind and low-vision climbers, guides, coaches and gym staff. In a preliminary gym evaluation, all ten blindfolded sighted expert climbers completed more of the route than with verbal guidance alone (p = .002), and their partners gave no hold-level directions.

Before my MFA, I received a Bachelor’s in Product Design from the University of Petroleum and Energy Studies, India, and completed a UX program at IIT Bombay. After it, I worked at Ecosphere Organics, a small materials startup in Detroit, where I researched turning agricultural bio-waste such as banana peels, corn husks and coffee grounds into biodegradable composites, testing compositions and exploring composites with embedded micro-sensors and reactive pigments that sense moisture, decay and temperature. I now work as an independent researcher.

Beyond research, I led UX for Vangard, a General Motors–sponsored self-driving car concept that GM shortlisted; co-created Motown Techno, a VR piece exhibited at Ars Electronica 2023; and designed Farmacy, a farming app nominated for a UX Design Award. Design taught me to build things; research is how I find out why they work.

The questions that stayed with me

I started by designing physical objects. Over time, I became more interested in the information they communicate, and in what happens when the system behind that information begins making decisions of its own.

  1. 2016–2020

    Physical product design

    During my Bachelor’s in Product Design, I worked through sketches, CAD, ergonomic studies, material experiments and physical prototypes. I learned that an object communicates before anyone reads an instruction: its shape suggests where to grip, its resistance signals how to move, and its physical feedback confirms an action.

    The question I carried forward

    How much can someone understand through physical interaction alone?

  2. 2020–2025

    Digital interaction design

    Moving into digital interfaces changed the problem. When I worked on Vangard, a General Motors–sponsored autonomous-vehicle concept, I was designing how a system’s perception and intentions could become understandable to passengers.

    My MFA thesis, TactileGrip, brought that question back into the physical world. A climbing hold could sense an approaching hand, communicate proximity and confirm contact without requiring a screen. Building and evaluating it showed me that sensing something accurately and communicating it effectively are two different problems.

    The question I carried forward

    How should a system translate what it senses into feedback a person can immediately interpret?

  3. 2025–present

    HCI research

    At Ecosphere Organics, I explored biodegradable materials embedded with sensing technologies. The work kept me close to physical computing, but my interest was shifting from what materials and devices could detect to what people should be told about it.

    In 2026, I began independent research on tactile communication in human–AI interaction. The problem has several parts: determining which answers can be encoded through vibration (Can a Buzz Answer That?), controlling unnecessary interruptions (TrueTap), and understanding how people interpret communicated uncertainty (Material Confidence).

    The question I’m pursuing next

    Can a wearable AI assistant make its information, timing and uncertainty understandable through touch, without taking over a person’s hearing or attention?

    That is the research direction I want to pursue through a PhD, developing and evaluating these systems with blind and low-vision communities.

Research: Adaptive Haptic Communication for Accessible Human–AI Interaction

What can touch communicate?

Whether a small vocabulary of vibration patterns can carry answers, spatial guidance or AI confidence that people can learn and interpret.

TactileGrip · Can a Buzz Answer That? · Material Confidence

When should a system communicate?

How sensing systems can put important information first, limit false alerts and avoid needless interruptions.

TrueTap · SenseShift

How should people act on uncertain assistance?

How felt uncertainty shapes reliance on AI, and how an assistant should say that it cannot tell.

Material Confidence · Can a Buzz Answer That?

All papers are sole-authored. Posted PDFs are submitted manuscripts under review, not peer-reviewed publications. Under review

PACM IMWUT Journal · submitted Nov 2026, under review

TrueTap: Budgeting How Often a Smartwatch Buzzes You by Mistake

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionHow can a smartwatch keep its false buzzes within a limit each wearer chooses?
  • ContributionA calibration method that sets the activity detector’s threshold so that only a chosen share of wearers go over their false-buzz budget, with a finite-sample guarantee. Released as a Python library and a browser runtime.
  • EvidenceOn day-long wrist recordings from 151 adults (CAPTURE-24), 3.7% of wearers went over budget, within the 9.8% bound, against 7.6% with a fixed threshold. Tested on three more datasets; a rerun from the raw recordings reproduced all 97,920 result rows (212 checks).
  • LimitationThe guarantee holds only when new wearers resemble the calibration wearers, and the method has not yet run on a watch or with users.

Submitted manuscript (PDF, anonymous review version)

ACM IUI 2027 Poster · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Can a Buzz Answer That? How Much of What Blind People Ask a Visual Assistant Fits a Vibration Vocabulary

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionHow many of the questions blind people ask a visual assistant could be answered by vibration instead of speech?
  • ContributionA small vibration vocabulary for yes, no, numbers, colours, “can’t tell” and “unsure”; rules for when to buzz and when to speak; and Felt Answers, an offline phone prototype that plays every rhythm.
  • EvidenceOf 8,000 held-out questions from blind people (VizWiz), 15.5% fit a rhythm and 26.8% more a felt “can’t tell”. A real vision–language model gave a confident answer on 20% of the photos people had marked unanswerable. One script rebuilds every number (49 checks).
  • LimitationNo one has felt the rhythms in a study yet, and touch was not reliably faster than speech.

Submitted manuscript (PDF)Poster (PDF)

ACM CHIIR 2027 Short Paper · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Material Confidence: Which Outcomes Can Tell Felt from Seen AI Confidence?

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionIf an AI’s confidence is felt as a vibration instead of seen on a screen, which study outcome can show whether people use it?
  • ContributionA design analysis that picks the outcome before any data are collected, plus a study protocol ready for preregistration, a web study app and band firmware.
  • EvidenceA re-analysis of a public dataset of 35,670 human–AI decisions (HAIID), then simulation. In simulated 96-person studies, reliance sensitivity detected use of the cue 99% of the time; the usual appropriate-reliance measure would need about 1,820 participants.
  • LimitationThe power results come from simulation and assume people read the vibration correctly 80% of the time. The study has not run, and no one has felt the patterns.

Submitted manuscript (PDF, anonymous review version)

Master’s thesis

MFA Thesis College for Creative Studies, 2023–24

Completed thesisResearch through designNot peer-reviewed

TactileGrip: Real-time Sensor-Embedded Climbing Holds for Non-Visual Route Navigation

Mihir Sharma · Thesis advisor: Predrag K. Nikolić

  • Winner, Thesis Select Award, College for Creative Studies, 2024
  • Nominee, UX Design Awards, New Talent, Berlin, 2024
  • QuestionCan climbing holds guide the hand directly, giving blind and low-vision climbers more independence from a guide’s spoken directions?
  • ContributionWorking holds with one cue for each moment: a beep that quickens as the hand approaches, a vibration on grip, a hold shape that points to the next hold, and star-shaped holds that announce progress aloud. Built with an Arduino Nano, an ultrasonic sensor read every 50 ms, a vibration motor and 3D-printed forms.
  • EvidenceDesigned from 20 interviews with blind and low-vision climbers, guides, coaches and gym staff. In a preliminary gym evaluation, all 10 blindfolded sighted expert climbers got further with TactileGrip than with verbal guidance alone (p = .002), and their partners gave no hold-level directions.
  • LimitationThe climbers were sighted and blindfolded. A counterbalanced study with 35 blind and low-vision climbers is specified but has not run.

Manuscript Full paper · in preparation

SenseShift: Adaptive AI‑to‑Tactile Communication for Blind and Low-Vision People

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionWhat should a navigation assistant tell blind and low-vision pedestrians, and how can it do so without competing with the sounds they rely on?
  • ContributionAn interruption policy that predicts how close each object will come, and a vibration code for a six-pod forearm band. Python and browser versions make identical decisions on 5,753 test frames.
  • EvidenceOn 1,000 held-out simulated walks it warned of 90.0% of hazards one to five seconds ahead, with 8.7% of messages about distractors, against 71.3% and 63.7% for announcing the nearest object.
  • LimitationAll results are computational. The band is designed but not built, and the three planned studies with blind and low-vision adults have not run.

DetroTune: Motown Techno, Detroit’s Music History in VR

Mihir Sharma, Raghunath Rajasekar, Siddhi Sakhare, Mahsa Khoshkbar Foroushan, Sara Fallahi

Exhibited at Ars Electronica Festival and Detroit Month of Design

  • QuestionCan spatial sound in VR teach a city’s cultural history better than video?
  • ContributionMotown Techno, our team’s piece in the Detro Tune exhibition: a VR journey through Detroit’s downtown and its techno music. I designed the spatial experience and built it in Unity with 3D sound and motion feedback.

  • LimitationA team project, compared only against video learning.

Mihir Sharma
